@graph.headline: Options vs Futures Trading: The Honest Comparison
@graph.description: Futures vs options compared honestly: obligation, margin vs premium, max loss for buyers and sellers, time decay, and which fits your risk, capital, and time.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between futures and options?

acceptedAnswer.text: Futures obligate both parties to transact at the agreed price at expiry unless squared off earlier — a commitment. Options give the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to transact at the strike, while the seller takes on the matching obligation and keeps the premium — a choice for the buyer, an obligation for the seller. That is the whole difference between futures and options in one paragraph, and everything else in this article is a consequence of it.

mainEntity.name: Which is better, futures or options?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither, in the abstract — which is better, futures or options, depends on your risk tolerance, capital shape, monitoring time, and purpose. A directional trader with daily monitoring time and margin discipline may suit futures' clean exposure; a trader who wants a defined worst case and accepts premium bleed may suit buying options; a hedger chooses between futures' symmetric offset and a protective put's flexible protection; an income seeker faces the uncovered-seller risk head-on. If you have no defined risk plan, the answer is neither yet — paper-trade and backtest first.

Only for buyers, and only in the worst-case sense — and that qualification is part of the answer, not a footnote. A bought option held to expiry generally caps the buyer's loss at the premium paid, while an uncovered call seller faces theoretically unlimited loss and a put seller faces large loss. Futures, meanwhile, have no premium floor: futures vs options risk differs because a futures loss can exceed initial margin many times over. So "which is safer" has no whole-instrument answer — it depends entirely on which side of the contract you are on.

mainEntity.name: Can you lose more than your margin in futures trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Margin is a performance bond, not a loss limit. In the illustrative example, a fall to Rs 700 produces a Rs 30,000 long-futures loss against an ILLUSTRATIVE Rs 20,000 initial margin — Rs 10,000 beyond the margin, with top-ups required along the way via daily mark-to-market settlement. Note the qualification: the long side's theoretical worst case is the full contract value if the underlying falls to zero, while the theoretically unlimited side is the short side. Either way, the margin posted is not the maximum you can lose.

mainEntity.name: Is the maximum loss in options really limited to the premium?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a bought option held to expiry, generally yes — if it expires worthless, the premium paid is the maximum loss. Before expiry, the realised loss depends on the sale price and remaining time value, so exiting early can lose less than the full premium. For sellers the answer is the opposite: uncovered sellers face large to theoretically unlimited loss, so the premium cap is a buyer-only statement, never a whole-instrument one.

mainEntity.name: Do futures have time decay like options?

acceptedAnswer.text: No option-style (theta) time decay — a futures price converges toward the spot price as expiry approaches and the futures-spot gap (basis) narrows, rather than a premium decaying to zero. But that is not "no time-related risk": the basis can still move against a trader or hedger before expiry. Time decay is an options-buyer cost; basis movement is the futures analogue to watch.

mainEntity.name: Which is better for beginners, futures or options?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is easy for a complete beginner, which is the honest options vs futures for beginners answer. Buying options caps the worst case but bleeds premium to time decay and volatility moves and is hard to get right consistently; futures give clean exposure but demand daily margin discipline and can lose more than the margin posted. Start with neither until a defined risk plan exists — paper-trade and backtest first. The step-by-step beginner path belongs to the not-yet-built beginners spoke, mentioned in plain text only.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between margin and premium?

acceptedAnswer.text: Margin is a returnable performance bond — a fraction of contract value, topped up on adverse moves — posted by futures traders and option sellers. Premium is the non-refundable upfront price paid by an option buyer for the right, kept by the seller whatever happens. One is a deposit against an obligation; the other is the price of a choice. Confusing them is how traders end up treating margin as a loss limit and premium as "cheap."

mainEntity.name: Can options sellers lose unlimited money?

acceptedAnswer.text: An uncovered call seller faces theoretically unlimited loss as the underlying rises without bound, because the seller must deliver the upside above the strike while keeping only the premium — the illustrative Rs 1,300 case costs the short call Rs 27,000 against Rs 3,000 received, growing rupee-for-rupee with further rises. A put seller faces large but bounded loss: strike × quantity minus premium received, if the underlying falls to zero. Covered or hedged sellers have different risk and are not covered by this statement.

mainEntity.name: Futures vs options for hedging: which works better?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on what is being protected. Futures give a symmetric, direct offset but give up favourable gains and carry basis risk, especially when an index contract hedges a single stock or quantities mismatch. A bought protective put caps downside for the premium while keeping upside above the strike, at the cost of premium bleed. For options vs futures hedging, choose the offset when you want a direct neutralisation and accept giving up gains, and choose the protective put — mentioned here only as a pointer to its staged spoke — when keeping the upside is worth paying premium for.

mainEntity.name: Do you need more capital for futures or options?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stated as funding shape, not a fixed ranking: an option buyer needs only the premium upfront to open the position, while a futures trader and an option seller need margin plus the ability to top it up on adverse moves, so their funding need is open-ended in a way the buyer's is not. But a large premium on a large quantity can exceed a small futures margin, so no absolute "futures need more capital" claim holds. Ask what shape of capital you can commit — fixed and capped, or open-ended with top-ups — rather than which instrument is "cheaper."

mainEntity.name: Should a beginner start with futures or options?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with neither until a defined risk plan exists; paper-trade and backtest first, using the live paper-trading and backtesting articles in plain text as your practice path, then match the instrument to your profile — directional exposure with margin discipline, defined worst case with premium bleed, hedging, or income with uncovered risk understood.
